beginner.headline: Using Technology for Job Applications
beginner.brief: Many young people use technology to help with job applications. They use it to write cover letters or CVs. This helps candidates send multiple applications at the same time. Now, companies receive large volumes of applications. Some managers do not blame them because the jobs market is difficult. However, some people use the technology to cheat on assessments. Employers still want to see the real personality of each person.

intermediate.headline: How AI Job Applications Can Backfire for Graduates
intermediate.brief: Recent graduates are increasingly using artificial intelligence to misrepresent themselves when they apply for jobs. One applicant explained that the process was exhausting and demoralising without some help from these tools. He thinks it is hypocritical for companies to ban artificial intelligence when they use it themselves. Meanwhile, a recent survey found that most employers have suspected applicants of misconduct during the selection process. One recruiter does not blame graduates for using these tools, given how brutal the current market is. However, she noted that this creates an unfair situation because some people use the programs heavily while others do not. To better judge applicants, companies are now relying on online assessments and video interviews. Employers stress that they still want to see true authenticity and diversity of thought in new recruits.

advanced.headline: How AI is Disrupting Graduate Job Applications
advanced.brief: Research suggests that university graduates are utilising artificial intelligence to distort their qualifications in job applications, though many argue they have little alternative. This software enables jobseekers to generate multiple simultaneous submissions—a tactic dubbed "spray and pray"—which intensifies competition in an already saturated recruitment sector. Applicants frequently utilise these tools to optimise their cover letters and identify the crucial buzzwords necessary to pass early-stage automated screening. This creates a delicate tightrope for applicants, who must sound human while still satisfying the rigid parameters of algorithmic filters. According to a recent survey, major UK employers are growing more tolerant of applicants using AI assistance during certain preliminary recruitment phases. Nevertheless, 92% of these employers suspected unethical practices, frequently observing individuals relying on real-time generative assistants during online video interviews. The overwhelming influx of applications recently prompted the energy corporation EDF to prematurely close its graduate scheme after receiving 12,000 entries. Recruiters caution that this discrepancy undermines a level playing field, advantaging those who exploit automation throughout the entire selection process. To counter this trend, EDF is striving to make its hiring procedures robust by delaying document reviews and prioritising behaviour-based assessments. Navigating this moral dilemma remains challenging for employers, who must grapple with automation while maintaining their standards for suitable new recruits.
